title: Keep Publishing, or Drink the Bacteria
actor_role: Registrar and research fellow in internal medicine at Fremantle Hospital; co-discoverer of the bacterium, and the person deciding whether to infect himself
t0: Mid-1984. Marshall and the pathologist Robin Warren have found spiral bacteria in the stomachs of most patients with gastritis and peptic ulcers, and published the association. The animal route has closed: a four-piglet study begun in January 1984 failed to establish infection and the animals outgrew the experiment. The conference abstract was rejected, senior colleagues are openly sceptical, and the grant panel for a randomised antibiotic trial was sceptical enough to fund only one probationary year. Marshall judges a trial that could settle the question to be years away. He can keep working the conventional path, or drink a concentrated culture of the bacterium himself -- without putting the plan to the hospital ethics committee -- to try to show directly that it infects and sickens a healthy person.
context_summary: Your theory is that a bacterium causes ulcers. Nearly everyone believes stomach acid does, and that nothing could live in a stomach anyway. The animal model failed, the abstract was rejected, and the trial that would prove it needs funding from people who do not believe you. You have a culture of the organism in the lab.
immediate_outcome: Marshall drank the culture after arranging a baseline endoscopy showing a healthy stomach, with informal help from his endoscopist Ian Hislop and the microbiology scientist Neil Noakes. He did not submit the plan to the ethics committee and did not tell his wife Adrienne in advance. Nothing happened for three days, then bloating, loss of appetite, morning vomiting without acid, and notably bad breath. An endoscopy on day 10 found active gastritis with biopsies positive for spiral bacteria and inflammatory cells. A second endoscopy on day 14 found the stomach lining recovering and -- unexpectedly -- no detectable bacteria in eight biopsy samples. He began the antibiotic tinidazole after that second endoscopy, by his own decision, and recovered fully.
long_term_outcome: The case drew real attention, including a July 1984 New York Times feature, and was formally reported in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1985. It did not end the field's scepticism. Acceptance built over roughly another decade through further clinical trials and epidemiology, culminating in a February 1994 NIH consensus conference endorsing antibiotic treatment for H. pylori-associated ulcers; Australia moved considerably faster than the United States. Marshall and Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the underlying discovery -- 21 years after the self-experiment, and resting on the accumulated later work rather than on it.
uncertainty_factors: What the organism would do to a healthy stomach was unestablished
Whether an N=1 result would persuade anyone
Whether ethics review would refuse, untested
Longer-term disease potential of the organism unknown

options.label: Keep to the conventional research path
options.short_description: Work within normal channels: publish further association studies, pursue ethics approval and grant funding for a properly randomised human antibiotic trial, and let accumulating data move opinion.
options.upside: Stays inside established research-ethics norms, risks nobody's health, and if a rigorous randomised trial eventually succeeds it produces far stronger and more broadly convincing evidence than any single case could.
options.downside: The funding and approval needed for a decisive trial are themselves gated by reviewers who doubt the theory. Meanwhile patients keep getting symptom-suppressing drugs or surgery for what Marshall believes is a treatable infection, and the theory -- and his career -- may be sidelined for years.
known_tradeoffs: This is the accepted standard for establishing a causal medical claim, and it is what most people around Marshall actually considered the responsible course; when he floated the self-experiment beforehand, several treated it as reckless rather than admirable. versus A diffuse but real cost: institutional inertia, more years of unnecessary antacid or surgical treatment for infected patients, and a genuine chance the theory keeps being dismissed as unproven before funding or attention arrives.

options.label: Drink the bacterial culture himself
options.short_description: Deliberately ingest a concentrated culture of the organism without submitting the plan to the hospital ethics committee, as the sole subject, to try to fulfil Koch's postulates by showing it infects a healthy person and causes disease.
options.upside: Could produce a fast, concrete, hard-to-dismiss demonstration in a previously healthy person, with consent resting on the one person able to weigh the specific unknown risk. And there is a fallback: a bismuth-plus-antibiotic regimen has already cleared the infection in his first four patients.
options.downside: Bypasses formal ethics review precisely because he expects refusal. What deliberate infection does to a healthy person is not established in 1984. And even a clean result is a single uncontrolled case, which cannot on its own show that eradicating the bacterium cures ulcers, or rule out something worse than gastritis.
known_tradeoffs: The animal route is exhausted, the trial pathway is realistically years off given the prevailing scepticism, and arguably only his own informed self-consent can authorise a risk that no ethics committee could confidently evaluate either -- because nobody yet knows what swallowing the organism does to a healthy stomach. versus Unknown personal health risk, the professional exposure of having gone around ethics review, and the scientific risk that an N=1 result will not be accepted as proof by a sceptical field whatever it shows.

case_information.content: Marshall and pathologist Robin Warren had identified spiral bacteria -- later named Helicobacter pylori -- in gastric biopsies and, in a roughly 100-patient study approved by the Royal Perth Hospital ethics committee, found them present in the large majority of patients with gastritis or peptic ulcers. Reported in 1983 Lancet letters and a fuller 1984 Lancet paper.

A four-piglet study Marshall ran with microbiologist Stewart Goodwin from January 1984 failed: the organisms did not colonise the piglets' stomachs, and the animals grew too large to continue before any usable disease model emerged.

The dominant medical view held that peptic ulcers were caused mainly by excess stomach acid, aggravated by stress, diet, smoking and alcohol. Most gastroenterologists believed no bacterium could survive the stomach's acidity and treated bacteria seen in gastric tissue as harmless commensals. This was the prevailing belief of the field, not an established fact.

An abstract on the bacteria-gastritis link submitted to the Gastroenterological Society of Australia's 1983 annual meeting was among the small minority rejected, and Marshall later recorded open scepticism and dismissive comments from senior colleagues in the months that followed.

Marshall later wrote of a hospitalised patient with unexplained gastric bleeding who tested strongly positive on his prototype antibody test but was treated with transfusions, acid-blockers and antacids rather than antibiotics, and ultimately underwent a total gastrectomy. He cited this as showing the practical cost of the theory not yet being believed. This is his own recorded account of what motivated him.

By the time he was planning the self-experiment, Marshall had already treated his first four Helicobacter-positive patients with a bismuth-plus-antibiotic regimen, achieving a 100% short-term cure rate on follow-up biopsy, and had shown in the laboratory that bismuth was directly toxic to the organism.

Cimetidine (Tagamet), the leading acid-suppressing H2-blocker, was generating roughly US $1 billion a year for Smith Kline & French by 1983, and ranitidine (Zantac) went on to sell more than $3 billion a year through most of the 1980s. Both relieved symptoms and allowed healing but did not treat an underlying infection, so ulcers typically recurred once treatment stopped.

Marshall's application to the NHMRC for a randomised trial of antibiotic versus standard ulcer treatment was, by his account, met with open scepticism and funded for only one probationary year. Giving experimental antibiotic therapy to ulcer patients ahead of stronger evidence was considered ethically premature under normal research standards, since proven treatments already existed.

Marshall later wrote that he considered submitting a self-experiment proposal to the ethics committee but concluded that if refused he would likely proceed anyway and lose the ability to publish or defend his job. He judged that only he could truly weigh and consent to the specific unknown risk, and went ahead without formal review, with informal and undocumented support from his endoscopist and microbiology colleagues. This is his stated reasoning, recorded afterward.

When Marshall raised the idea of human self-infection with senior colleagues beforehand, his microbiology chief David McGechie laughingly declined an informal invitation to try it himself, and Marshall's later accounts describe colleagues generally regarding the plan as reckless rather than admirable.

The infection would produce documented acute gastritis, confirmed by endoscopy and biopsy on day 10, but appear to clear on its own by day 14 -- before any antibiotic was started. Marshall has called this 'a mystery to this day.'

A widely repeated version of the story has Marshall's wife insisting he take antibiotics as soon as he fell ill. In his own 2005 Nobel lecture he states this was not really the case: he decided independently to end the experiment and start tinidazole only after the day-14 endoscopy, and notes that tinidazole alone would not have been an effective cure anyway.

It would take roughly another decade of clinical trials, epidemiology and international debate -- not the self-experiment alone -- before the 1994 NIH consensus conference formally endorsed antibiotic treatment for H. pylori-associated ulcers.

Marshall and Warren would receive the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 21 years later, for the discovery and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease -- a recognition resting on the accumulated subsequent research rather than on the 1984 self-experiment in isolation.

Later immunological research would associate widespread eradication of H. pylori in some populations with rising rates of certain allergic and autoimmune conditions, leading some researchers to suggest the organism may also have had immune-modulating effects alongside its harms. This complicates a simple 'harmful bacterium' story, and was neither knowable nor relevant in 1984.

evidence.title: Source disagreements recorded in the research record
evidence.author_or_institution: Research record for this case (see src-01 through src-10)
evidence.supported_claim: Two points. First, the popular claim that Marshall took antibiotics on his wife's orders: his own 2005 Nobel lecture explicitly says this was not really the case -- he decided independently after the day-14 endoscopy, by which point biopsies were already negative. This record follows his primary account and flags the popular version as a myth worth correcting. Second, the exact date: the Nobel lecture narrates the sequence without giving a calendar date, and while secondary sources converge on July 1984 and some add 'a Tuesday morning', no primary contemporaneous record fixes the day, so this case says circa July 1984 rather than asserting one.
